libertine

LIB-er-teen · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Libertine is having a disregard for morality.

The count's reputation as a libertine was built on decades of scandalous parties and broken promises.

Example

The novel's central character is a wealthy libertine who drifts from one broken engagement to the next without a hint of guilt.

A pattern of pleasure-seeking with total disregard for the moral rules everyone else follows -- broken engagements, no guilt -- is exactly what libertine describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hedonist: A hedonist is devoted to pleasure -- filling life with whatever feels good -- and being one breaks no rules by itself. A libertine goes further: the pleasure-seeking comes with deliberate defiance of moral rules, crossing lines on principle rather than merely enjoying things.

profligate: A profligate is recklessly wasteful and over-indulgent, burning through money and pleasures without restraint. A libertine may spend carefully; what marks a libertine is willful disregard of moral rules, especially around pleasure -- the defiance, not the wasting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ascetic: practicing strict self-discipline and self-denial

puritanical: following strict moral or religious rules

Where it sits · how far moral limits are abandoned — carefree → libertine → debauched

carefree vs. libertine: Someone carefree is simply relaxed and unworried; a libertine actively disregards moral rules, especially around pleasure.

debauched vs. libertine: Debauched pushes libertine even further, suggesting a pattern so extreme it has caused real, visible ruin.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — liber

root — liber: free (Latin (liber))

suffix — -tine

suffix — -tine: one who/pertaining to (Latin (libertinus))

Put it together

Put it together: The root liber- ('free') plus the ending -tine (from libertinus, originally 'a freed slave') gives a word for someone who claims total freedom from moral rules.

Use the root in a new word: liberty

Use the root in a new word: liberty: Liberty shares the same liber root as libertine -- one is simple freedom, the other is freedom taken to a morally reckless extreme.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Libertine specifically implies defying moral rules on principle, often around sex or excess. Hedonist is a close cousin that focuses purely on pleasure-seeking, without necessarily implying intentional moral defiance.
